name: ESCAPADE
operator: NASA / UC Berkeley Space Sciences Laboratory / Rocket Lab
short_status: Operating as of 28 October 2026: both orbiters are being tracked, Blue 1.04 million km and Gold 1.16 million km from Earth and falling back towards it, loitering since their 13 November 2025 launch. The burns for Mars are planned for 7 November (Blue) and 9 November (Gold), arrival September 2027.
tagline: NASA / UC Berkeley Space Sciences Laboratory / Rocket Lab · United States · Orbiter · 2025 · Multipolar Mars Operating
stats: identical orbiters, Blue and Gold, flying as a single mission
cost of the whole mission per JPL Horizons; English Wikipedia's $75m total includes the launch
from Earth on 28 October 2026 and falling back towards it, still more than ten months from Mars

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 13 November 2025, 20:55 UTC (3:55 p.m. EST), from Launch Complex 36 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, on the second flight of Blue Origin's New Glenn (NG-2). Sources disagree by ten minutes: NASA's own launch blog gives 3:55 p.m. EST and English Wikipedia sharpens it to 3:55:01 p.m. EST (20:55:01 UTC), the seconds coming from Wikipedia rather than from NASA, while the spacecraft record inside JPL Horizons says 20:45 UTC. The Horizons trajectory files themselves start at 21:31 UTC (Blue) and 21:32 UTC (Gold), which is spacecraft separation rather than liftoff.

facts.label: Catalogue identities
facts.value: ESCAPADE-Blue is 2025-260A (JPL Horizons body -9) and ESCAPADE-Gold is 2025-260B (Horizons -10). The New Glenn upper stage that carried them is catalogued separately as 2025-260C (Horizons -9901495), so a Horizons search for the mission name returns three objects, not two.

facts.label: Where they were on 23 August 2026
facts.value: Horizons, queried on 23 August 2026, put Blue 2,337,000 km from the centre of the Earth and Gold 2,352,000 km out, about 33,000 km apart. Re-queried on 28 October 2026, on kernels revised 19 October 2026 that carry real tracking data through 12 October for both spacecraft, Horizons returns the same figures. Navigation data says nothing about the health of the spacecraft, but it does mean both vehicles were being tracked as recently as 12 October and their trajectories updated on 19 October. Note where that is: on 23 August 2026 the pair sat about 88 degrees away from the Earth-Sun L2 direction, and Blue was only some 80,000 km further from the Sun than Earth itself. They were not at L2 on that date. The loiter is a wide loop that passes through the L2 region, closest to it around the start of March 2026 (2 March for Blue, 5 March for Gold), lines up with the L2 direction once more around 30 June 2026, only about 550,000 km from Earth, and swings far to the side of the Sun-Earth line the rest of the time.

facts.label: Each spacecraft
facts.value: 535 kg fuelled, 209 kg dry. Stowed 1.20 by 1.65 by 1.09 m, 4.88 m long deployed thanks to a 2 m magnetometer boom. Fixed solar arrays giving about 800 W at Earth and 260 W at Mars, 128 W drawn by the science payload, two star trackers, four fine Sun sensors, four reaction wheels, and a 60 cm fixed X-band dish. JPL Horizons names the bus a Rocket Lab Photon; English Wikipedia calls it a Rocket Lab Explorer, the Photon derivative marketed for interplanetary work.

facts.label: Telling them apart
facts.value: The two are physically identical, so the practical difference is radio: Blue downlinks at 8417.165797 MHz and Gold at 8423.148147 MHz.

facts.label: Instruments
facts.value: Four per spacecraft, eight in total: EMAG, a magnetometer from NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center; EESA, an electrostatic analyser from UC Berkeley's Space Sciences Laboratory; ELP, a Langmuir probe from Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University; and VISIONS, a visible and infrared camera from Northern Arizona University.

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: English Wikipedia gives $75 million total, split as $55 million for the two spacecraft and their instruments and $20 million for the New Glenn launch. The JPL Horizons spacecraft record describes it as a low-cost mission of under $80 million. Both figures are far below the $582 million cited for MAVEN, the previous NASA orbiter built to study the same question.

facts.label: Who builds and runs it
facts.value: Principal investigator Robert Lillis of UC Berkeley's Space Sciences Laboratory, which leads the mission, working with Rocket Lab (spacecraft), Advanced Space, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Blue Origin and NASA. It flies under NASA's SIMPLEx line of small planetary missions.

facts.label: Why two spacecraft
facts.value: A single orbiter cannot separate a change in time from a change in place. Flying two identical instrument sets at controlled separations lets the team measure how solar wind energy and momentum move through the hybrid magnetosphere Mars makes without a global magnetic field, and how atmosphere escapes through it.

facts.label: The route to Mars
facts.value: Not a direct transfer. The pair was launched to a loiter that JPL Horizons and NASA both describe as being around the Earth-Sun L2 point roughly 1.5 million km out, where they spend about a year taking space weather data. In practice the Horizons trajectory is a much wider loop, ranging from about 0.55 to 2.5 million km from Earth and lining up with the L2 direction only twice, briefly: around the start of March 2026, about 2 million km out, and around 30 June 2026, only about 550,000 km out. A low-altitude perigee burn in November 2026 sends them onto a cruise of about ten months (the Horizons record says 11) with one major and several minor corrections along the way. Horizons' prediction of 19 October 2026 puts the perigees about 1,660 km above Earth for Blue on 7 November and about 1,010 km for Gold on 9 November, the dates Space.com reported in January; English Wikipedia gives a lower figure, within 600 km.

facts.label: First images
facts.value: The VISIONS cameras returned their first frames on 21 November 2025, eight days after launch: one spacecraft photographed the edge of its own solar panel in visible and infrared light, the other photographed deep space. NASA said the visible channel looked sensitive enough to catch Martian aurora from orbit.

facts.label: The one known problem
facts.value: In early December 2025 the operations team saw low thrust during a trajectory correction burn on one of the two spacecraft and stood the manoeuvre down while engineers investigated. NASA said on 15 December 2025 that the other spacecraft had completed both of its corrections as planned, and on 7 January 2026 that the delayed second correction had been completed on 6 January. NASA has not said which spacecraft it was or what caused the low thrust, but the mission log kept by Rocket Lab, which built both spacecraft, shows the late finisher was Gold: Blue made its second correction in mid-December, and Gold completed its own second correction, a 97.7-second burn, on 6 January 2026, after a seven-second firing on 24 December.

facts.label: Arrival plan
facts.value: The two arrive at Mars a few days apart in September 2027, each firing for about 11 minutes into a large capture orbit of roughly 60 hours, then spending several months trimming down, with science orbits reached by mid-2028 in NASA's plan. Science Campaign A flies both in the same 170 by 8,400 km orbit, 5.66 hour period, 65 degree inclination, at varying separations; the JPL Horizons record prints the apoapsis as 18,400 km, which does not fit a 5.66 hour period.

facts.label: The split
facts.value: After six months in formation, Blue drops to a 7,000 km apoapsis and Gold rises to 10,000 km. The different periods (4.9 and 6.6 hours) make the orbits precess at different rates in Mars's lumpy gravity field, so the two drift apart and sample distant parts of the magnetosphere at the same moment. That campaign runs five months. Horizons says this ends the nominal science mission less than three years after launch, but the UC Berkeley mission design page has science beginning in late spring 2028, which carries the six-month and five-month campaigns into 2029.

facts.label: How current this entry can be
facts.value: NASA's ESCAPADE blog has not been updated since 7 January 2026, and the UC Berkeley mission site carries no dated 2026 status posts we could retrieve, but NASA has published two ESCAPADE articles elsewhere on its science site since then. On 26 February 2026 it said the science instruments were all operating as of 25 February, and on 24 July 2026 it released Earth and Moon images that one spacecraft took on 3 July from 584,600 km away. On 8 October 2026 UC Berkeley's news office said the two would make their final pass close to Earth in early November and fire their engines towards Mars. The Horizons navigation product revised on 19 October 2026 carries tracking through 12 October for both spacecraft. As of 28 October 2026 we found no NASA statement on the spacecraft newer than the July article, and this entry claims no more than these sources support.

timeline: ESCAPADE loses the free ride it was designed around. It had been selected as a low-cost ride-along to Mars with the Psyche spacecraft, but Psyche's launch went to Falcon Heavy on a higher-energy Mars flyby that ESCAPADE could not use, and NASA decided to buy the mission its own launch rather than cancel it.
Blue Origin wins the launch for about $20 million, and the mission is manifested on the very first flight of New Glenn, then targeted for October 2024.
The two spacecraft arrive at the Cape for launch processing.

NASA stands down from the October 2024 launch. The stated reason is not the rocket's readiness but the propellant: with a fuelled spacecraft and a planetary window that turns small slips into months, NASA chose to avoid the cost, schedule and technical problems of having to defuel. The next opportunity was described as spring 2025 at the earliest.
Two launch attempts are scrubbed, the first for cumulonimbus cloud, the second for a solar storm.

Launch at 20:55 UTC on New Glenn flight NG-2 from LC-36. The booster, GS1-2-1 (named Never Tell Me The Odds), lands on the platform vessel Jacklyn about 600 km offshore in the Atlantic. A Viasat InRange technology demonstration flew on the same launch.
First images from the VISIONS cameras, eight days after launch: a solar panel edge in visible and infrared, and a deep space frame from the other spacecraft.

NASA reports that one spacecraft produced low thrust during a trajectory correction burn and that the manoeuvre has been delayed while engineers investigate. The other has completed both of its corrections.

NASA reports that the delayed second trajectory correction was completed on 6 January. It is the last post on NASA's ESCAPADE blog; NASA's later updates, on 26 February and 24 July 2026, appeared as articles elsewhere on its science site.

JPL Horizons publishes revised trajectory kernels for both spacecraft, with real tracking data through 12 October for both. On 28 October Blue is about 1.04 million km from Earth and Gold about 1.16 million km, both falling back towards Earth.

Planned: the pair leaves the loiter, dives to a low perigee and fires the trans-Mars injection burns, Blue on 7 November and Gold on 9 November in Horizons' prediction of 19 October 2026 (perigees about 1,660 km and 1,010 km up), starting a cruise of about ten months.

Planned: arrival at Mars a few days apart, each with an insertion burn of about 11 minutes into a roughly 60 hour capture orbit, followed by several months of orbit trimming before science begins in 2028.
